lessons.title: Build a clear sentence
lessons.summary: Practise the basic shape of a sentence and put an idea in a useful order.
learning_outcomes: Recognise a complete sentence
Arrange words into a clear sentence
Write one focused sentence
lessons.introduction: A clear sentence usually communicates one main idea. In English, a common starting pattern is subject + verb + object or complement. Longer details can follow once the core idea is clear.

example.label: Example
example.explanation: The subject comes before the verb. The object tells the reader what was built.

exercises.prompt: Which option is a complete sentence?

options.label: Because the team tested the feature.

exercises.explanation: This option has a subject (the team) and a verb (tested), and it expresses a complete thought.

exercises.prompt: Arrange these parts into a clear sentence.
exercises.explanation: Start with the subject, follow with the action, then add what was built and the context.

exercises.prompt: Write one clear sentence about something you built, learned, or practised.
exercises.guidance: Keep one main idea. Include a specific action or subject. This response is saved for your review; it is not automatically graded.

lessons.title: Grammar in context
lessons.summary: Choose verb forms and prepositions that fit the meaning of a sentence.
learning_outcomes: Choose a verb form for a completed action and a future plan
Use articles and common prepositions in context
Review grammar without losing the intended meaning
Notice and revise a common tense error in a sentence
lessons.introduction: Grammar choices depend on what you mean and when an action happened. Read the whole sentence before choosing a form. The goal is to make the meaning clear, not to memorise isolated rules.

example.label: Example
example.before: Yesterday, I build a login page.
example.after: Yesterday, I built a login page.
example.explanation: “Yesterday” places the action in the past, so “built” fits the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that correctly describes a completed action yesterday.
exercises.explanation: “Tested” is the simple past form and matches the time marker “yesterday”.

exercises.prompt: Choose the most natural preposition: “I am responsible ___ testing the API.”
exercises.explanation: The usual construction is “responsible for” followed by a noun or an -ing verb.

exercises.prompt: Write a sentence about a task you completed recently. Include when you did it.
exercises.guidance: Check that the verb form matches the time you mention. This is a self-review prompt, not an automated grammar grade.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct article: “I built ___ small dashboard for the project.”
exercises.explanation: Use “a” before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound when it is mentioned for the first time.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that clearly describes a plan for tomorrow.

options.label: Tomorrow, I shared the test results.
Tomorrow, I will share the test results.
Tomorrow, I sharing the test results.

exercises.explanation: “Will share” is a clear way to describe a future plan. Context and intended meaning guide tense choice.

exercises.prompt: Correct the tense in this sentence while keeping its meaning: “Yesterday, she go to the lab and check the results.”
exercises.guidance: Look for the time word “yesterday”. Use past-tense forms for both actions. This open response is saved for self-review; Prepped does not automatically mark grammar corrections.

lessons.title: Structure a project summary
lessons.summary: Explain what problem a project addresses, what you built, and who it is for.
learning_outcomes: State the problem in one sentence
Describe a concrete feature or approach
Identify the intended users
lessons.introduction: A useful project summary gives the listener a map: the problem, your approach, and the people the work is intended to help. Avoid claiming impact that you have not measured.

example.label: Example
example.before: It is an app with many useful features.
example.after: The app brings campus notices and student discussions into one place so students can find updates more easily.
example.explanation: The revised example names the product's purpose and intended users without claiming a measured outcome.

exercises.prompt: Which opening gives the clearest problem statement?

options.label: My project is very innovative and useful.
Students may need to check several channels to find campus updates.

exercises.explanation: It describes a concrete user problem. Technologies belong in the approach, not the problem statement.

exercises.prompt: Arrange these parts into a useful project-summary sequence.

tokens.label: The approach or feature I built
Who the project is intended for

exercises.explanation: Start with the problem, explain the approach, then identify the intended users.

exercises.prompt: Write a three-part project summary: problem, what you built, and intended users.
exercises.placeholder: The problem is… I built… It is intended for…
exercises.guidance: Use only facts you can support. If you have not measured an outcome, describe the intended benefit rather than claiming success.

lessons.title: Make explanations specific
lessons.summary: Replace vague claims with a concrete example and distinguish implementation from measured results.
learning_outcomes: Replace vague wording with a specific detail
Give a concrete example
Avoid presenting an unmeasured outcome as fact
lessons.introduction: Words such as “good”, “fast”, and “useful” can be unclear without context. A specific explanation names the feature, action, test, or observation. Keep intended outcomes separate from results you have actually measured.

example.label: Example
example.before: The application is very reliable and helps everyone.
example.after: I added input validation and tested the session API with the automated test suite. I have not yet measured usage with students.
example.explanation: The revised version names implementation and test evidence, and clearly states what has not been measured.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is most specific and appropriately cautious?

options.label: My application is the best solution for all students.
I added input validation and tested the profile API with automated tests.

exercises.explanation: It identifies concrete work and a verifiable check without claiming universal impact.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the explanation from implementation to evidence to limitation.

tokens.label: I added input validation to the endpoint.
The automated tests cover valid and invalid input.
I have not yet tested the flow with a group of students.

exercises.explanation: Describe what you implemented, what you checked, and what remains unverified.

exercises.prompt: Describe one feature you worked on, how you checked it, and one limitation that remains.
exercises.placeholder: I implemented… I checked it by… I have not yet…
exercises.guidance: Name a real feature and a real check. Do not invent test results, user feedback, or impact.

lessons.title: Choose useful words in context
lessons.summary: Use context to choose precise words and common word combinations.
learning_outcomes: Use context clues to choose a word
Prefer specific wording over vague wording
lessons.introduction: A word is useful when it fits the meaning and situation. Read the whole sentence, notice the surrounding clues, and choose wording that communicates the intended idea.

example.label: Example
example.before: I did a big work on the app.
example.after: I completed a substantial amount of work on the app.
example.explanation: The revised wording uses a more natural phrase for describing effort.

exercises.context: A teammate asks what you changed in a project. You added checks that reject invalid form submissions.
exercises.prompt: Choose the most precise verb: “I ___ input validation to the form.”
exercises.explanation: “Implemented” is precise for adding a technical feature. “Made” and “did” are less specific here.

exercises.context: Choose the phrase that sounds natural in a project update.
exercises.prompt: Which phrase is most natural?

options.label: I made a research about the issue.
I carried out research into the issue.
I did researchation for the issue.

exercises.explanation: “Carry out research” is a common collocation. The other options are not natural English.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite one vague sentence about your studies or project using a more specific word.
exercises.guidance: Keep the original meaning. Choose a precise verb or noun; do not add achievements that did not happen.

lessons.title: Listen for the key detail
lessons.summary: Practise identifying one important detail in a short spoken project update.
learning_outcomes: Listen for a concrete detail
Distinguish the task completed from a future plan
lessons.introduction: In a short conversation, listen for the action and its status. A completed task, a current activity, and a future plan are different kinds of information.

example.label: Listening strategy
example.after: Listen for the action, the object, and time/status words such as “completed”, “currently”, and “next”.
example.explanation: These clues help you identify what has happened and what is only planned.

exercises.audio_text: I finished adding input validation to the registration form yesterday. Today, I am testing the error messages. Next, I plan to review the form with two classmates.
exercises.transcript: I finished adding input validation to the registration form yesterday. Today, I am testing the error messages. Next, I plan to review the form with two classmates.
exercises.prompt: What did the speaker finish yesterday?

options.label: Adding input validation to the registration form

exercises.explanation: The speaker says input validation was finished yesterday. Testing is happening today, and the classmate review is a future plan.

exercises.audio_text: The API tests pass on my machine. I have not yet run the tests in the deployment environment, so that check is still pending.
exercises.transcript: The API tests pass on my machine. I have not yet run the tests in the deployment environment, so that check is still pending.
exercises.prompt: Which statement is supported by the spoken update?

options.label: The deployment environment has been fully tested.
The API tests pass locally, but deployment testing is pending.
The API has no remaining issues.

exercises.explanation: The speaker reports a local test result and explicitly says deployment testing has not happened yet.

exercises.prompt: In one or two sentences, summarise the difference between a completed task and a planned task in the audio.
exercises.placeholder: The speaker completed… The next planned task is…
exercises.guidance: Use details from the spoken message. You may reveal the transcript if you need the text alternative.

lessons.title: Record your starting point
lessons.summary: Complete four short tasks. Your responses are saved as a baseline; no proficiency level or total score is assigned.
learning_outcomes: Record a current sentence-structure response
Record a current listening-comprehension response
Save a short project explanation for later comparison
lessons.introduction: This is a low-stakes starting-point check, not an exam. Answer using what you can do today. Prepped stores your responses and task completion so you can revisit them later; it does not certify an English level or predict placement outcomes.

exercises.prompt: Which option is a complete sentence?
exercises.explanation: A complete sentence communicates a full thought. This check records the response; it does not assign a proficiency level.

exercises.prompt: Arrange these parts into a clear project explanation.
exercises.explanation: A useful explanation starts with the need, describes your action, then gives evidence or a check.

exercises.audio_text: I completed the login form validation yesterday. Today I am checking the error messages. Next, I plan to test the form with a classmate.
exercises.transcript: I completed the login form validation yesterday. Today I am checking the error messages. Next, I plan to test the form with a classmate.
exercises.prompt: What did the speaker complete yesterday?

options.label: Testing the form with a classmate

exercises.explanation: The completed task was login form validation. Error-message checks are happening today; the classmate test is planned next.

exercises.prompt: Describe one project or technical task you have worked on. Include the problem, what you did, and how you checked it.
exercises.placeholder: The problem was… I worked on… I checked it by…
exercises.guidance: Use your own current ability. If you have not measured a result, say what you checked and what remains unknown. You may type or record a response.

lessons.title: Shape a sentence for clarity
lessons.summary: Expand, combine, shorten, and clarify sentences without changing the intended meaning.
learning_outcomes: Add relevant detail to a basic sentence
Combine related ideas clearly
Shorten a sentence without losing its key meaning
lessons.introduction: A sentence can be expanded with useful detail, combined with a related idea, or shortened to remove repetition. Keep the main meaning intact. Prefer concrete information over extra words.

example.label: Example
example.before: I made the app better by doing many things.
example.after: I added form validation and tested three invalid inputs.
example.explanation: The revision replaces a vague claim with a specific action and check.

exercises.prompt: Which revision adds useful detail without changing the original fact? Original: “I tested the form.”

options.label: I tested the form with three invalid email inputs.
I tested the form perfectly and proved it has no bugs.
I tested everything in the entire application.

exercises.explanation: It adds a specific test detail. The other options make claims that the original sentence does not support.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the parts into one clear sentence using “because”.
exercises.explanation: The reason follows the result and is joined with “because”.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this sentence to make it shorter and clearer without changing its meaning: “Due to the fact that the server was not responding, I was unable to access the page.”
exercises.guidance: Keep the cause and result. A possible direction is to replace “due to the fact that” with “because”. This is self-review, not an automatic writing grade.

lessons.title: Ask clear questions
lessons.summary: Form useful yes/no and information questions for study, teamwork, and clarification.
learning_outcomes: Choose a clear question form
Use do, does, and did with the base verb
Ask a polite clarification question
lessons.introduction: Questions help you check meaning, ask for missing information, and keep a conversation moving. In many present-simple questions use do or does; for past questions use did and the base form of the main verb. Wh-words such as what, when, where, why, and how identify the information you need.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct question about a teammate's daily task.

options.label: What does she work on each morning?
What she does work on each morning?
What do she works on each morning?

exercises.explanation: Use “does” with “she”, followed by the base verb “work”.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct question about yesterday's test.

options.label: Where did you tested the API?
Where did you test the API?
Where you did test the API?

exercises.explanation: After “did”, use the base form “test”.

exercises.prompt: Write one polite question you could ask when a project requirement is unclear.
exercises.guidance: Ask about one specific missing detail. Keep the tone respectful and the question easy to answer.

lessons.title: Use useful study and project phrases
lessons.summary: Learn collocations and practical phrases, then create an example from your own work.
learning_outcomes: Recognise common study and project collocations
Choose phrases that fit a professional context
Create and review a learner-authored example
lessons.introduction: Some English words commonly appear together. Learning a phrase as a unit can make communication more natural. Notice the situation, meaning, and grammar around the phrase. Adapt examples to work you have actually done.

exercises.context: You are describing how you checked a software feature before sharing it.
exercises.prompt: Choose the natural collocation: “I ___ a series of tests before the demo.”
exercises.explanation: “Carry out tests” is a natural collocation meaning to perform tests.

exercises.context: A teammate says, “I will look into the error and update you.”
exercises.prompt: What does “look into the error” mean here?
exercises.explanation: “Look into” means investigate or examine something to understand it.

exercises.prompt: Choose one phrase—“carry out a test”, “look into an issue”, or “make progress”—and write a true sentence about your studies or project.
exercises.guidance: Use the phrase naturally and keep the example factual. You can save a useful phrase later when the revision feature is available; this response remains part of this lesson attempt for now.

lessons.title: Follow a short conversation
lessons.summary: Listen for the request, the response, and the next action in a brief team conversation.
learning_outcomes: Identify a speaker's request
Distinguish a response from a future action
Summarise the agreed next step
lessons.introduction: In a conversation, listen for who is speaking, what they need, and what happens next. Replay the message if useful. You can reveal the transcript at any time; the text alternative is equivalent learning content, not a penalty.

exercises.audio_text: Riya: The search page works, but the results take too long to appear. Arjun: I will check the database query first. Riya: Great. Please share what you find before our afternoon review.
exercises.transcript: Riya: The search page works, but the results take too long to appear. Arjun: I will check the database query first. Riya: Great. Please share what you find before our afternoon review.
exercises.prompt: What does Riya ask Arjun to do before the review?

options.label: Share what he finds after checking the query

exercises.explanation: Arjun will check the query, then share what he finds before the afternoon review.

exercises.audio_text: Meena: Have you finished the login tests? Dev: The valid-login cases pass. I still need to test expired passwords. Meena: Please add that result to the test notes when it is done.
exercises.transcript: Meena: Have you finished the login tests? Dev: The valid-login cases pass. I still need to test expired passwords. Meena: Please add that result to the test notes when it is done.
exercises.prompt: Which test is still pending?
exercises.explanation: Dev says valid-login cases pass, but expired-password testing remains.

exercises.prompt: Summarise the agreed next action from either conversation in one or two sentences.
exercises.guidance: Mention the person, action, and timing if the audio provides them. Reveal the transcript if you need the text alternative.

lessons.title: Give a clear short response
lessons.summary: Practise describing a task, explaining a process, and retelling a short update in your own words.
learning_outcomes: Describe a task with context and action
Explain a simple process in order
Retell a short update in the learner's own words
Explain how a feature was checked and describe the observed result
lessons.introduction: A clear spoken response can use three simple parts: context, action, and detail. You do not need complicated vocabulary. Speak at a comfortable pace, pause between ideas, and use the optional recording only if you want to review a transcript. Prepped does not grade fluency or confidence.

exercises.prompt: Describe a task you completed recently. Include the context, what you did, and one specific detail.
exercises.placeholder: I was working on… I… One detail is…
exercises.guidance: You may type or record. Keep the response to three or four sentences. Use only details that are true for you.

exercises.prompt: Explain a simple process you know—for example, how you test a form or prepare for a class. Describe the steps in order.
exercises.guidance: Use sequence words such as first, then, after that, and finally. A listener should be able to follow the steps.

exercises.prompt: Explain how you checked one feature in a project and what you observed. Separate what you tested from what you have not tested yet.
exercises.placeholder: I checked… I observed… I have not yet…
exercises.guidance: Describe one real check and its observed result. State any important limitation; do not claim that a test proves the whole application is error-free.

exercises.prompt: Retell this update in your own words: “The first version is ready. The team found two issues during testing. We will fix them before sharing the next version.”
exercises.guidance: Keep the three facts: first version ready, two issues found, fixes planned before sharing. Do not add an outcome that was not stated.

lessons.title: Express an opinion and handle a follow-up
lessons.summary: Practise giving a reason, an example, and a relevant response to a follow-up question.
learning_outcomes: State an opinion and support it with a reason
Add a relevant example
Respond to a follow-up without changing the original point
lessons.introduction: A useful opinion response states your view, gives a reason, and adds an example. A follow-up may ask you to explain a choice or consider another option. It is fine to pause and clarify the question before answering.

exercises.prompt: Which is more useful when learning a new programming tool: reading documentation first or trying a small example first? Give your opinion and one reason.
exercises.guidance: There is no single correct opinion. State your preference and support it with a relevant reason or example.

exercises.prompt: Follow-up: Someone prefers the other approach. How would you acknowledge their view and explain when it might be useful?
exercises.placeholder: That approach can be useful when… I prefer… because…
exercises.guidance: Acknowledge the alternative fairly. Explain a situation where it helps, then restate your own reason without dismissing the other person.

exercises.prompt: Write a polite sentence you could use if you did not understand a follow-up question.
exercises.guidance: Ask for clarification directly and respectfully. You are practising a communication strategy, not being graded.

lessons.title: Listen, repeat, and self-review
lessons.summary: Practise a model phrase at a comfortable pace and review what you can hear clearly.
learning_outcomes: Listen to a model phrase and use the text alternative
Repeat a short phrase at a comfortable pace
Choose one self-review focus without receiving an automated pronunciation score
lessons.introduction: Listen to the model phrase, then repeat it at a comfortable pace. You may record a spoken version if you want a transcript to edit, but speech recognition can make mistakes. Compare your attempt with the written phrase and choose one small thing to practise. Prepped does not calculate pronunciation, accent, phoneme, or fluency scores.

exercises.audio_text: I tested the application, corrected the error, and explained the result to my teammate.
exercises.transcript: I tested the application, corrected the error, and explained the result to my teammate.
exercises.prompt: Listen to the phrase, then repeat it once or twice at a comfortable pace. Focus on finishing each word clearly.
exercises.guidance: Use Play spoken message, then repeat the phrase. You can record and edit a transcript or simply practise privately. Notice word endings and pauses; do not try to imitate an accent or force a faster pace.

exercises.audio_text: Could you explain that step again, please?
exercises.transcript: Could you explain that step again, please?
exercises.prompt: Listen and repeat this polite clarification question. Try pausing naturally before “please”.
exercises.guidance: Listen, repeat, and compare with the text. Choose one thing to practise again, such as a comfortable pace or a clear final word. No pronunciation score is produced.

exercises.prompt: What one part of the phrase would you like to practise again: pace, pauses, word endings, or a particular word?
exercises.guidance: This is a private self-review choice. It is not an assessment of your accent, pronunciation accuracy, or confidence.
